title: Moonlight in the Moon
summary: The song's images are a ḍamaru of compassion that plays while Āryadeva shines, supportless, and moonlight shining in the moon, as the mind's transformation enters 'there'; around them, the poet does not know where the self has gone, and he gives up fear, disgust and worldly custom to look and look at emptiness. Munidatta reads the song as entry into clear light: the self is the king of mind, whose conceptual thoughts dissolve like moonlight into the setting moon, compassion is conventional bodhicitta and the ḍamaru's sound the unstruck sound (cp.31.m2, cp.31.m3, cp.31.m4). He reads the last couplet as the poet's praise of himself for having made all the corruption of saṃsāra fruitless (cp.31.m6).

flags.note: The poet's name is not in the heading line itself: Shastri prints the attribution āryadevapādāḥ ('the venerable Āryadeva') before 1a, from which the input removes it. Following the brief (a heading names rāga and poet) I give it here, in the glossary form 'Āryadeva' without the honorific -pāda. The Tibetan heading names the poet too ('phags pa lha'i zhabs kyi'o). Drop it if you prefer the heading to carry only what Shastri prints there.

lines.gloss: where (in which) · mind · senses · wind · become · lost

flags.note: Shastri prints ho ṇa ṭhā. I read ho ṇaṭhā, 'become lost' (ṇaṭhā from Prakrit ṇaṭṭha, Sanskrit naṣṭa): it gives ho a sense, rhymes with paiṭhā, 'entered' (praviṣṭa), at the end of 1b, and fits Munidatta's paraphrase that objects, winds and senses are made without intrinsic nature (cp.31.m2). With the printed division: 'where mind, senses and wind do not stay' (ṭhā from sthā, 'stand'). My transliteration shows my division.

The Tibetan line has gang la yid dang dbang po rlung rnams zhugs gyur na, 'when mind, senses and winds have entered that in which': 'entered' where the Bengali has ho ṇa ṭhā. It may follow Munidatta's tatra praviṣṭe sati ('when it has entered there', cp.31.m2) rather than a different Bengali reading. I translate the Bengali.
The pa of [pa]baṇa is Shastri's restoration of damaged text; Munidatta's pavana (cp.31.m2) and the Tibetan rlung, 'wind', support it.

lines.translit: ṇa jānami apā kam̐hi gai paiṭhā
lines.gloss: not · (I) know · self · where · gone · entered
lines.en: I do not know where the [self]{atman} has gone and entered.

flags.note: Apā (from ātman through Prakrit appā) is taken as 'the self', the subject of 'gone and entered'. It can also be reflexive: 'I do not know where I myself have gone'. The Tibetan line (bdag gis mi shes gang du song dang gang du sleb) makes bdag, 'I', the one who does not know. Munidatta reads apā as the king of mind (cp.31.m2); per the glossary that stays out of the line and goes in a note.

Kam̐hi gai paiṭhā: two participles, 'where (it) went (and) entered'; the Tibetan has 'where it went and where it arrived'. 'Has gone and entered' is literal; 'where it has gone in' would be smoother but drops a verb.

Akaṭa is obscure; Munidatta glosses it āścarya, 'wonder' (cp.31.m3), the Tibetan line has ya mtshan, and the glossary files it under adbhuta. It may be an exclamation (my choice, 'A wonder:') or an adjective, 'wondrous', with compassion (so the Tibetan comment, rmad du byung ba'i snying rje) or with the ḍamaru.

Karuṇā ḍamaruli taken as 'the ḍamaru of compassion' (a compound), with bājaa intransitive, 'plays, sounds'. 'Compassion plays the ḍamaru' is possible but less likely with bājaa. The -li of ḍamaruli may be a diminutive.

Ṇirāse is filed under niralamba, 'supportless', on the strength of Munidatta's nirālambena (cp.31.m3) and the Tibetan dmigs pa med la. The Old Bengali itself looks more like nirāśa, 'without hope or desire', or nirāśraya, 'without support'. The -e may be locative ('shines in the supportless', as the Tibetan la takes it) or instrumental (Munidatta's nirālambena); I used a bare predicate, 'shines, supportless', to leave both open.

lines.gloss: in the moon · moonlight · as · shines (appears)

flags.note: Cāndare taken as locative, 'in the moon'. Munidatta cites the line as cānder ityādi (cp.31.m4), which may point to a genitive, 'the moon's moonlight'; re could also be a vocative or emphatic particle. The locative gives the image that 3b ('enters there') answers.

The Tibetan line has zla ba zla ba'i 'od zer ji bzhin yongs su shes, with yongs su shes, 'fully knows' or 'is fully known', where the Bengali has patibhāsaa, 'shines, appears' (pratibhāsate). The Tibetan sense is unclear to me; I follow the Bengali.

Munidatta's simile has moonlight absorbed back into the moon once the moon has set (cp.31.m4). The song says only that moonlight shines (or appears) in the moon; the setting is not in the line and stays in the note.

Bikaraṇe taken as nominative (the eastern -e), 'the mind's transformation', subject of 'enters'. It could be instrumental or locative: 'the mind, by (or in) transformation, slips and enters there'. Whether bikaraṇa means the mind's changing states or the act of changing is unclear; Munidatta puts the series of conceptual thoughts in its place (cp.31.m4), which the glossary keeps out of the line.

The Tibetan line has sems kyi rnam 'gyur de la 'phangs nas yongs su zhugs, 'the mind's transformation, cast into that, fully enters': 'phangs, 'thrown', where the Bengali has ṭali, which I take from ṭal-, 'slip, move, waver'.

lines.gloss: having given up · fear · disgust · worldly custom

flags.note: The Tibetan line has srid pa'i skyug bro, 'the disgust of existence', where the Bengali has bhaya ghiṇa, 'fear, disgust'. Its translators probably read bhava, 'existence', which differs from bhaya by one letter. I keep 'fear': the Bengali has it, Munidatta's Sanskrit has bhaya (cp.31.m5), the Tibetan comment on this couplet has 'jigs pa dang ngo tsha ba, 'fear and shame', and the Tibetan of 5b has 'jigs pa, 'fear'. The glossary has no entry for fear, so I propose one (bhaya); if you would rather not have an entry, strip the markup.

Bhaya ghiṇa loācāra has no conjunction. It may be three things given up, or 'fear and disgust, (that is,) worldly custom'. Munidatta and the Tibetan comment take fear and the rest as the world's conduct itself (cp.31.m5). I kept the asyndeton, 'fear, disgust, worldly custom', so as not to decide.

Munidatta cites the verb as chāṛila, 'gave up' (finite past), where the edition has chāṛia, 'having given up' (cp.31.m5); his paraphrase has parityaktaḥ, the Tibetan line spangs gyur, the Tibetan comment spangs nas.

The couplet has no finite verb. Suṇa biāra may be 'the examination of emptiness' (so the Tibetan line, blta zhing lta bas stong pa nyid la rnam par dpyad, 'by looking and looking, examined emptiness') or 'empty on examination', nearer Munidatta's 'being is seen as empty' (cp.31.m5); suṇa may be the adjective 'empty'. The glossary's noun 'examination' keeps me from writing 'I examined emptiness'; the line is verbless as a result.
Cāhante: 'looking' (Munidatta's nirīkṣaṇa, 'gazing', cp.31.m5; the Tibetan blta), though Bengali cāh- also means 'want, seek': 'seeking and seeking'.

Bihariu is the least certain word in the song. (1) My choice: vihṛta, 'taken away, removed'. The agent is in the instrumental (ājadebem̐), which calls for a transitive verb with saala, 'all', as object, and Munidatta paraphrases 'all the corruption of saṃsāra was made fruitless' (cp.31.m6). (2) The commoner sense of vi-hṛ, 'roam, sport': 'Āryadeva has roamed through all', a picture of siddha conduct. (3) The Tibetan line, 'phags pa lha ni kun la rnam par dpyod par byed, 'Āryadeva examines everything', as if reading biāriu (vicārita). That would rhyme closely with ṇibāriu and echo biāra in 4b.

Ṇibāriu (nivārita), 'warded off', is a past participle with Āryadeva of 5a as its agent; I render it as an absolute phrase ('driven far off') rather than add a second 'has'. No conjunction in the source: 'and' is added for English. The Tibetan ('jigs pa dang ni skyug bro ring du zad par byas, 'fear and disgust were ended far off') has fear here, which supports bhaya in 4a.

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music. The heading names the rāga to which the song is sung, Paṭamañjarī; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) transcribes the name as pa Da ha many+dza ri.

Shastri's edition prints āryadevapādāḥ, 'the venerable Āryadeva', before the first line. It is an attribution, not part of the verse, and is given here in the heading. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) heads the song as the melody pa Da ha many+dza ri 'of 'phags pa lha'i zhabs' (Āryadevapāda), and Munidatta opens by saying that Āryadevapāda, delighted, sets out the same meaning (cp.31.m1). The poet names himself in the refrain (2b) and again in the last couplet (5a).

Shastri prints the refrain cue ধ্রু after couplet 1 as well as after couplets 2 to 5. Munidatta names couplet 2 as the refrain (dhruvapada, cp.31.m3) and counts couplets 3, 4 and 5 as his second, third and fourth verses (cp.31.m4, cp.31.m5, cp.31.m6), so the refrain is couplet 2.

Shastri prints ho ṇa ṭhā. This draft reads ho ṇaṭhā, 'become lost', taking ṇaṭhā from Prakrit ṇaṭṭha (Sanskrit naṣṭa); it rhymes with paiṭhā, 'entered' (praviṣṭa), at the end of 1b. With the printed division the line would say that mind, senses and wind 'do not stay' (ṭhā from sthā, 'stand'). Munidatta's paraphrase says that objects, winds, senses and the rest are made without intrinsic nature (cp.31.m2). The pa of [pa]baṇa is Shastri's restoration; Munidatta's pavana and the Tibetan rlung, 'wind', support it.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has gang la yid dang dbang po rlung rnams zhugs gyur na, 'when mind, senses and winds have entered that in which', with 'entered' where the Bengali has ho ṇa ṭhā. Munidatta's comment speaks of entering there (tatra praviṣṭe sati, cp.31.m2), and the Tibetan line may follow it rather than a different Bengali reading.

Apā comes from Sanskrit ātman, 'self', through Prakrit appā. It can also be reflexive, 'oneself', which would give 'I do not know where I myself have gone'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bdag gis mi shes, 'I do not know', making bdag, 'I, self', the one who does not know.

Munidatta places the couplet in clear light (prabhāsvara), in which, by the sequence of withdrawing the maṇḍala and the like, objects, winds, senses and the rest are made without intrinsic nature. He reads apā as the king of mind (cittarāja): once it has entered there, the poet does not know where it has gone (cp.31.m2). The Tibetan comment likewise speaks of the king of mind (sems kyi rgyal po).

Ḍamaru: a small drum shaped like an hourglass, with two heads, sounded by beads on cords that strike the heads when the hand twists it; Śiva, kāpālika ascetics and tantric deities carry it. The song's ḍamaruli may add a diminutive ending, 'little ḍamaru'.

Akaṭa is an obscure word. Munidatta glosses it āścarya, 'wonder, wondrous' (cp.31.m3), and the Tibetan line has ya mtshan, 'wonder'. It may stand as an exclamation, as in this draft, or qualify compassion or the ḍamaru; the Tibetan comment takes it with compassion: 'wondrous compassion' (rmad du byung ba'i snying rje).

Munidatta says that with the refrain the poet makes joy firm. He reads compassion as conventional bodhicitta, which comes through the guru's lineage, and says the ḍamaru makes the unstruck sound; Āryadeva shines through the supportless yoga in which no phenomenon is apprehended (cp.31.m3). A sentence about the unstruck and knowledge is obscure in the Sanskrit; the Tibetan has the knowledge of the unstruck sound realized.

Munidatta renders ṇirāse as nirālamba, 'without support or object' (cp.31.m3), and the Tibetan line has dmigs pa med la, 'in the objectless'. The Old Bengali could also reflect nirāśa, 'without hope or desire', or nirāśraya, 'without support'. The ending -e may be locative, 'in the supportless', as the Tibetan takes it, or instrumental, as in Munidatta's nirālambena.
The couplet is a simile (jima, 'as'): moonlight shining in the moon is set beside the mind's transformation slipping and entering 'there'. The song does not say where 'there' is.

Munidatta says this couplet, his second verse, states the true nature of objects. His simile: as moonlight is absorbed back into the moon once the moon has set, so when the king of mind goes to no-mind and enters clear light, its series of conceptual thoughts dissolves right there. He adds a scriptural verse: as the moons in the water are withdrawn when the moon sets, so, when the mind has dissolved in the innate, all the faults of conceptual thought perish (cp.31.m4). The setting moon is his; the song says only that moonlight shines in the moon.

Munidatta cites the line as cānder ityādi (cp.31.m4), which may point to a genitive, 'the moon's moonlight', where the edition has cāndare, taken here as locative, 'in the moon'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has zla ba zla ba'i 'od zer ji bzhin yongs su shes, with yongs su shes, 'fully knows' or 'is fully known', where the Bengali has patibhāsaa, 'shines, appears'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sems kyi rnam 'gyur de la 'phangs nas yongs su zhugs, 'the mind's transformation, cast into that, fully enters', with 'phangs, 'thrown', where the Bengali has ṭali, 'slipping'. Munidatta's paraphrase puts the series of conceptual thoughts (vikalpāvalī) where the song has the mind's transformation, without an explicit gloss (cp.31.m4); the Tibetan comment cites rnam 'gyur.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has spangs gyur srid pa'i skyug bro 'jig rten spyod pa rnams, 'given up: the disgust of existence, worldly conduct', with srid pa'i, 'of existence', where the Bengali has bhaya, 'fear'; its translators perhaps read bhava, 'existence', which differs from bhaya by one letter. The Tibetan of 5b ('jigs pa, 'fear'), the Tibetan comment on this couplet ('jigs pa dang ngo tsha ba, 'fear and shame') and Munidatta's Sanskrit (bhaya, cp.31.m5) all have fear, which this draft keeps. Munidatta cites the verb as chāṛila, 'gave up', where the edition has chāṛia, 'having given up'.

Munidatta says this couplet, his third verse, states that being is partless. He paraphrases: I, the siddha master, have given up the conduct of the world, fear, shame and the like; by gazing along the path of the guru's words, 'empty': being is seen in the form of selflessness (cp.31.m5). He takes fear and the rest as the worldly custom itself, and names shame (lajjā) where the song has disgust.

The line has no finite verb. Suṇa biāra may be 'the examination of emptiness', as the Tibetan line takes it (blta zhing lta bas stong pa nyid la rnam par dpyad, 'by looking and looking, examined emptiness'), or 'empty, on examination', nearer Munidatta's 'being is seen as empty' (cp.31.m5); suṇa may be the adjective 'empty'.

Munidatta calls the last couplet, his fourth verse, the poet's praise of himself: by the true guru's grace, in making the dharma of selflessness manifest, Āryadevapāda has made all the corruption of saṃsāra fruitless (cp.31.m6). The Tibetan comment has him refute all the faults of saṃsāra and make them fruitless.

Bihariu is uncertain. With the agent in the instrumental (ājadebem̐) a transitive verb is expected; this draft takes it as vihṛta, 'taken away, removed', which suits Munidatta's paraphrase, 'all the corruption of saṃsāra was made fruitless' (cp.31.m6). The commoner sense of the verb, 'roam, sport', would give 'Āryadeva has roamed through all'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'phags pa lha ni kun la rnam par dpyod par byed, 'Āryadeva examines everything', as if reading a form of vicār-, 'examine' (it renders biāra in 4b with the same verb); such a form would rhyme closely with ṇibāriu in 5b. For 5b the Tibetan has 'jigs pa dang ni skyug bro ring du zad par byas, 'fear and disgust were ended far off'.

termsOmitted.reason: Tibetan only: the Tibetan line has 'phangs nas, 'having thrown', where the Bengali has ṭali, rendered 'slips'. The English follows the Bengali; the difference is in a witness flag and note.
Tibetan only: the Tibetan line has srid pa'i, 'of existence', where the Bengali has bhaya, 'fear'. The English follows the Bengali (see the witness flag and the proposal bhaya).
Tibetan only: the Tibetan line has rnam par dpyod par byed, 'examines', where the Bengali has bihariu, rendered 'has done away with'. The English follows the Bengali; the alternatives are flagged.

proposals.definition: Fear (Old Bengali and Sanskrit bhaya; Tibetan 'jigs pa). Song 31 twice names it with disgust (ghiṇa) as what the poet gives up (4a) and drives far off (5b). Munidatta counts fear and shame among the world's conduct that the siddha master has given up (cp.31.m5). The Tibetan of 4a has srid pa, 'existence', instead.
proposals.rationale: Song 31 uses the word twice, always paired with disgust (ghṛṇā, already an entry), and the glossary has no entry for fear. With one, the pair can be linked consistently, and fear stays distinct from bhava, 'existence', the reading the Tibetan line of 4a seems to reflect. Fear also recurs in the commentary (bhaya-lajjā here, fear of death in song 22). The regex keeps whole words only, so abhaya and bhayaṅkara do not match.

questions: 4a: I translate bhaya as 'fear' against the Tibetan srid pa'i ('of existence'), on the evidence of the Bengali, Munidatta's Sanskrit, the Tibetan comment and the Tibetan of 5b. With no glossary entry for fear, I proposed one (bhaya) and marked both occurrences. Do you want the entry, or plain unmarked 'fear'?
1a: should we adopt my division ho ṇaṭhā, 'are lost' (rhymes with paiṭhā, suits Munidatta's 'made without intrinsic nature'), or keep Shastri's printed ho ṇa ṭhā, 'do not stay'?

5a: bihariu. I chose 'has done away with everything' (transitive, as the instrumental ājadebem̐ suggests, close to Munidatta's 'made fruitless'). Would you prefer 'has roamed through all' (the ordinary sense of vi-hṛ), or a note giving the Tibetan 'examines everything'?

4b: the glossary's noun 'examination' for vicara leaves the line verbless ('looking and looking: the examination of emptiness'). May I use an inflected surface, as in '[examined]{vicara} [emptiness]{sunyata}', or should the nominal line stand?

Heading: I added the poet, as '· Āryadeva' (glossary form, without the honorific -pāda that the manuscript's attribution has), although Shastri prints the attribution before 1a and not in the heading line. Keep it?
2a: is 'A wonder:' as an exclamation acceptable for akaṭa, or would you rather follow the Tibetan comment's 'wondrous compassion' (e.g. 'The ḍamaru of wondrous compassion plays')?
2b: 'supportless' follows the approved niralamba rendering and Munidatta. Should the note say more plainly that the Old Bengali ṇirāsa looks like nirāśa, 'without hope or desire'?

3b: the glossary gives vikarana as 'transformation'. Fine for the line, or would 'changes' ('the mind's changes slip and enter there') read better, given the doubt over whether the word names states or a process?
